title: PYRREGULAR: Unified Framework for Irregular Time Series
one_liner: A single standardized format and benchmark lets researchers compare methods for predicting patterns in time series data where measurements arrive at uneven intervals and times.
lead: Real-world data often arrives at irregular intervals: a patient's blood pressure is checked at random times, traffic sensors miss readings, climate stations record on different schedules. Different research fields have invented fragmented solutions, making it hard to compare methods or apply lessons across domains. PYRREGULAR solves this by creating one universal format and a repository of datasets so researchers can benchmark classifiers on equal ground.

paras: When a sensor records data at irregular intervals — say, a hospital monitoring a patient's heart rate, or a weather station logging rainfall on days it rains — existing methods struggle. A naive approach is to ignore the irregular spacing and treat all measurements equally, which loses critical information about WHEN events happened. Another common trick is to fill in missing values by guessing what would have happened in between, but guessing can corrupt the data with false patterns.

Worse, researchers in different fields have each invented their own ad-hoc solutions. A healthcare researcher writes code for medical time series; an environmental scientist writes separate code for climate data. The same classifier ideas are never compared fairly across domains because datasets and formats don't match. No one can agree on what 'irregular time series classification' even means.

callout.html: PYRREGULAR creates one shared data format and benchmark so all researchers can test and compare irregular time series classifiers on the same datasets.

paras: Before PYRREGULAR, each research community stored irregular time series in its own format (one used sparse arrays, another stored gap-lengths, a third interpolated values). No two looked alike. PYRREGULAR's move is to settle on one shared format: (timestamp, value) pairs in a standard array structure. This simple unification is the paper's core contribution — not a new algorithm, but a common language.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: classification accuracy under irregular spacing
hidden.name: per-classifier accuracy score
paras: The paper measures one core quantity for each classifier on each dataset: what fraction of the time series it correctly predicted the label. This is the classic accuracy metric — count correct predictions, divide by total. But the hidden insight is that the paper reveals which classifiers handle irregular spacing well (high accuracy despite gaps and uneven timing) versus which ones do not. A naive method that ignores the irregular intervals should score lower than a method that respects timing.

Each of the 12 classifiers gets tested on all 34 datasets. The paper reports an accuracy score for every combination, creating a grid of 12 by 34 numbers. A researcher looking at this grid can see: does this classifier work best on medical data? Is it hopeless on climate data? Do timing-aware classifiers always win, or sometimes does a simple baseline surprise everyone? These patterns are hidden in the grid until someone runs the full benchmark.

heat.caption: Darker means higher accuracy on irregular time series; highlighted cells are classifiers that respect irregular timing.

reads.html: Look at the grid: which classifier wins most often? Does it stay strong across all domains, or is it specialized?
The paper reports mean accuracy, standard deviation, and per-dataset breakdown, letting readers see both the overall winner and the variance.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: the power of a shared benchmark
paras: The core mechanism is simple: when multiple methods compete on the same dataset with the same metric, the best one emerges because there is nowhere to hide. A classifier that works in healthcare might fail on climate data because climate events have different patterns. A method that ignores timing will lose to one that respects it, if the irregular intervals truly matter. Before PYRREGULAR, each research community published results on its own datasets with its own metrics, so no one could see these real differences. A healthcare researcher would report 92% accuracy on their dataset and declare victory; a climate researcher would do the same on theirs. Were the methods equally good, or was one dataset just easier? Nobody knew.

PYRREGULAR creates a level playing field. Every classifier sees the same data, the same rules, the same metric. This forces the true rankings to surface. Moreover, the shared repository means new researchers can add their own classifiers to the benchmark without collecting data from scratch — they inherit 34 datasets instantly. This accelerates progress because researchers spend time on methods, not data collection.

math.words: For each classifier on each dataset, accuracy equals the count of correct label predictions divided by the total count of time series in that dataset.
math.equation: accuracy_c_d = (# correct predictions by classifier c on dataset d) / (# total time series in dataset d)
symbols: the dataset (e.g., medical heartbeat, climate rainfall)
count of time series where the predicted label matched the true label
count of all sequences in the dataset

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Dataset: 100 medical time series, each labeled 'healthy' or 'diseased'.
Classifier A guesses 78 correctly, 22 wrongly. Accuracy = 78 / 100 = 0.78 (78%).
Classifier B guesses 85 correctly, 15 wrongly. Accuracy = 85 / 100 = 0.85 (85%).
On this dataset, Classifier B is better; but PYRREGULAR tests both on 34 datasets, so we see if B stays strong everywhere or if A is better on climate data.

math.note: The paper repeats this calculation for all 12 classifiers and 34 datasets, building a grid of 12 by 34 accuracy numbers that reveals which methods handle irregular timing best.

bars.h2: How the benchmark surfaces real differences

charts.title: Without PYRREGULAR (fragmented)
charts.note: Three teams, three datasets, three metrics. Are the methods equally strong or is one dataset just easy? No comparison possible.

charts.title: With PYRREGULAR (unified)
rows: Weighted-focus 17 points higher because it respects timing
charts.note: Same classifier tested on all 34 datasets with the same metric. True winner emerges; new researchers can compare fairly. The weighted-focus method beats the baseline because it learns which time steps matter most, so it ignores gaps gracefully and recovers patterns from uneven timestamps.

items.html: If 30 of the 34 datasets are medical and only 4 are climate, a method tuned for medical data will look artificially strong in the benchmark. The paper should report per-domain breakdowns.
If a dataset's labels are mislabeled (a 'healthy' patient marked 'diseased'), all classifiers will train and test on corrupted ground truth, leading to meaningless scores.

If one classifier had its hyperparameters (learning rate, number of layers) carefully tuned on these specific datasets and others did not, the tuned one will score higher for a shallow reason, not superior method.
PYRREGULAR provides code and a public repository, so other researchers can verify results, add new classifiers, and extend the benchmark fairly. Transparency and reproducibility prevent most gaming.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A convincing demo takes PYRREGULAR's public repository, picks three classifiers (e.g., naive baseline, weighted-focus, recurrent), downloads a few of the 34 datasets, runs each classifier on each dataset, and plots accuracy scores. The demo should show that different classifiers score differently, and that at least one classifier's strength or weakness is visible across multiple datasets (not a fluke on one dataset). This proves that the benchmark successfully measures real differences in how well methods handle irregular time series.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_per_classifier = mean( [# correct / # total for dataset 1, # correct / # total for dataset 2, ...] )
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss: with a shared format and benchmark, you can finally see which classifier truly handles irregular timing best, instead of guessing from three separate papers.
